transcript:
00:00 Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. We've got Diego our SE who will take most of the SDK walkthrough.
00:08 Tom Nguyen: Hey thanks, appreciate it, we got Priya and Avery on the call as well. We're excited to see the quickstarts, last time we talked we were evaluating latencies for checkout personalization.
00:18 Diego Ramos: Awesome, quick agenda, run through Python quickstart, TypeScript example, auth and env setup, then run a live sample request and show Console traces. Sound good?
00:27 Priya Shah: Yep, good. Quick note on security: we need SOC2 report and KMS integration details, also SSO for admin console.
00:36 Maya Patel: We'll share SOC2 and SSO docs after the call, Sam from security can chime in later if needed.
00:42 Diego Ramos: Ok jumping into the Python quickstart. The repo is a tiny sample, requirements.txt with redwood-sdk, we show both API-key flow and OIDC flow. In code you do from redwood import Client... (laughs) I keep saying Redwood like the tree.
00:58 Tom Nguyen: (laughs) that's fine. Question: do you support implicit token rotation? We want short-lived creds.
01:06 Diego Ramos: Yes, we support short-lived JWTs via our private deployment and the hosted tokens can be rotated programmatically. We'll show the env var pattern: REDWOOD_API_KEY or REDWOOD_OIDC_TOKEN.
01:20 Avery Miles: For our infra, we run in a VPC and have an internal NAT, will the hosted API be allowed? We probably need Private deployment for customer data.
01:30 Maya Patel: Right, good callout. You can choose hosted API for speed, Dedicated if you want reserved capacity, or Redwood Private for VPC / on-prem. For Siren Retail at scale and data residency you probably want Private or Dedicated.
01:45 Diego Ramos: Back to the code: here's the sample request, client.generate(model="redwood-2-small", prompt=..., max_tokens=128). We also show streaming using the SDK event hooks. The TypeScript example is almost identical, just import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference' (note: name in demo is approximated).
02:05 Tom Nguyen: Any gotchas with Node and streaming? Our stack is Node 18 with serverless lambdas.
02:12 Diego Ramos: Streaming works in Node but watch cold starts and keep-alive. For serverless we recommend a warm pool or using Dedicated for steady throughput. Also batching is limited by lambda memory/cpu.
02:30 Priya Shah: Can you show the Console? We'd like to see cost per token breakdown and traces for a sample route.
02:37 Diego Ramos: Sure, flipping to Console, redwood console shows per-route token counts, latency P95, and model mappings. Here's a route called /personalize-checkout mapped to redwood-2-medium in the demo tenant. You can pin versions and set fallback policies. 
02:55 Maya Patel: Diego, can you show an example fallback policy?
03:00 Diego Ramos: Yep. Policy example: primary -> redwood-2-medium, fallback -> redwood-2-small, and region fallback to eu-west-1 if primary region saturated. That keeps availability.
03:16 Sam Lee: How do audit logs look? We need full request metadata for compliance but not full user PII in stored prompts.
03:24 Diego Ramos: Audit logs include request id, route, user id (if you forward it), model, duration, tokens. You can redact or filter PII before sending. With Private you can also opt out of retention; we support configurable retention windows.
03:40 Tom Nguyen: For local dev, what's the recommended workflow? We want simple integration tests.
03:45 Diego Ramos: Use the quickstart with a local mock server, set REDWOOD_API_KEY to the test key, and run unit tests against recorded fixtures. For end-to-end perf, run load tests against a Dedicated staging pool.
03:58 Priya Shah: Can you cover Redwood Optimize briefly? We have tight cost targets.
04:05 Diego Ramos: Sure. Redwood Optimize will analyze your traffic and give batching, cache, and model/quantization recs. For example, if you have repeated prefixes we suggest prefix caching (KV cache) to avoid re-encoding tokens; it can cut token costs significantly.
04:20 Maya Patel: Diego will include a suggested quantization profile in the benchmark run.
04:25 Diego Ramos: Quick demo now: live request from Python quickstart. I'm going to run the sample payload Tom shared earlier. (typing) Ok sending.
04:40 System: [audio glitch]
04:45 Diego Ramos: Response came back in 180ms p50, p95 was 420ms — these numbers are demo env, not final.
04:55 Tom Nguyen: That's promising. Our SLO is 200ms p95 for personalization. How close can you get?
05:04 Diego Ramos: Depends on model size, sequence length and whether you have dedicated capacity. For p95 200ms we often recommend a small/medium quantized model on Dedicated with warm KV cache, and colocated region. We'll propose configs.
05:22 Priya Shah: On encryption, we need KMS-managed keys for model input at rest. How does Redwood integrate with our KMS?
05:30 Maya Patel: For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; for hosted we support customer-managed keys in supported clouds. We'll attach the security doc.
05:42 Tom Nguyen: When you say KV cache can you explain briefly? We want to know what we store and for how long.
05:49 Diego Ramos: KV cache stores transformer key/value states for prefixes so you don't re-run the full prefix. It is ephemeral in memory by default; you can persist to redis for cross-instance warmup. You control ttl and whether to persist any user tokens — you should avoid storing PII.
06:10 Avery Miles: For on-prem, is there a flavors of deployment that are air-gapped?
06:15 Maya Patel: Yes, we offer an on-prem package for regulated customers, and we can do an air-gapped install with an offline bundle. That comes with the Private plan and enterprise support.
06:26 Diego Ramos: Ok next, auth code snippet for TypeScript. Example: const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.generate(...). We also show OIDC exchange flow with short-lived tokens.
06:40 Tom Nguyen: Do you have SDK samples that integrate with KMS to decrypt tokens at runtime?
06:46 Diego Ramos: We don't ship KMS clients, but the sample repo shows how to fetch a key from AWS KMS and set the env var before process start; for rotation you can use a sidecar or ephemeral token service.
06:58 Priya Shah: Any rate-limiting primitives? We need per-tenant quotas and circuit breakers.
07:05 Maya Patel: We support per-route quotas, token quotas, and per-API-key throttles. You can also set fallback rules to a lower-cost model when thresholds are hit.
07:18 Diego Ramos: Back to live demo, I'm toggling tracing on in Console so you can see a sample trace with token breakdown. See the waterfall: tokenizer time, attention kernel time, kv cache hit. (minor stutter)
07:40 Tom Nguyen: Nice, that token breakdown is helpful for ops. Do you expose per-token cost in the UI?
07:46 Diego Ramos: Yes, per-route cost and token-level breakdown are visible in Console and via the billing API.
07:55 Priya Shah: For our procurement, we need pricing for Dedicated and cost model for spinning burst capacity.
08:02 Maya Patel: We'll send pricing options: reserved monthly commit and burst tier pricing. Also include dedicated sizing guidance based on your QPS.
08:12 Diego Ramos: Quick note: quantization profile can change accuracy slightly; we'll include eval prompts to validate quality before rolling out.
08:22 Tom Nguyen: How does rollback work if a model upgrade regresses?
08:27 Diego Ramos: Console supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback. You can pin previous model version to route with a single click. Also we keep eval regression alerts tied to your prompt sets.
08:42 Priya Shah: Anything we should do to prepare for the benchmark?
08:45 Diego Ramos: Send sample payloads, expected concurrency, desired latency SLOs, and a couple of eval prompt sets. We'll run the benchmark on a staging Dedicated pool and share results and recommendations.
08:58 Maya Patel: I'll capture those as action items.
09:02 Tom Nguyen: I have one more security question — SSO for admin console. Does Redwood support SAML and SCIM?
09:09 Maya Patel: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM user provisioning are supported for Enterprise accounts. We'll share the SSO integration doc.
09:18 Diego Ramos: Wrapping up the SDK differences — Python is synchronous-friendly and great for batch jobs; TS/Node is good for edge and streaming. We recommend the same model selection logic for both.
09:33 Priya Shah: Ok great. Any blockers from your side to sign off a POC?
09:38 Tom Nguyen: We just need security docs and pricing, and we'll confirm sample payloads. Timeline target: pilot in two weeks.
09:45 Maya Patel: Sounds good. We'll send repo, security docs, pricing and propose a POC kickoff on 2026-08-11.
09:54 Diego Ramos: I'll prepare the benchmark runbook and quantization suggestions.
10:00 System: Meeting ended

Note: transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., "K-V cash" instead of KV cache, "sam-el" for SAML) and speaker overlaps typical of call exports.
